lumbar.emergency.name: Emergency Protocol
lumbar.emergency.desc: Use this when you feel acute pain. Don't train, just do this.
lumbar.emergency.ex0.note: Decompress the spine immediately. Maximum relief.
lumbar.emergency.ex1.note: Release the piriformis and relax the sciatic nerve.
lumbar.emergency.ex2.name: Child's Pose with traction
lumbar.emergency.ex2.note: Arms extended forward. Let gravity decompress.
lumbar.emergency.ex3.name: Slow Cat-Cow (20 reps)
lumbar.emergency.ex3.note: Increase disc circulation. Feel each vertebra.
lumbar.emergency.ex4.name: Deep Hip Flexor Stretch
lumbar.emergency.ex4.note: Remove the anterior pull on the lumbar spine.
lumbar.morning.name: Morning Routine (Pre-work)

lumbar.morning.ex0.name: Cat-Cow Warm-up
lumbar.morning.ex0.note: Wake up the spine before stressing it.
lumbar.morning.ex1.note: Counteract the overnight shortening of the psoas.
lumbar.morning.ex2.name: Glute Bridge activation
lumbar.morning.ex2.note: Activate glutes before they fall asleep sitting.
lumbar.morning.ex3.note: Prepare the whole body for sedentary work.
lumbar.morning.ex4.note: Mobilize the thoracic area before hunching.
lumbar.pausa25.name: Active Break 2 min (every 25 min)
lumbar.pausa25.desc: The automatic break system will alert you. Maximum impact in minimum time.
lumbar.pausa25.ex0.name: Stand up and move

feature.indexTitle: Nine features that talk to each other.
feature.indexLead: Training, food, cardio and community connected by the same progress. Open any of them to see how it works before you create an account.
feature.training.name: Guided training
feature.training.card: Phase-based guided programs, free sessions and a catalog of 1,578 exercises you can filter by equipment and muscle.
feature.training.metaDesc: A phased program with your week already laid out and a session that walks you set by set, with timed rest and 1,578 exercises to pick from.
feature.training.h1: Open the app. Today's session is already set.
feature.training.heroLead: You pick a program once and the app takes care of the rest: it splits your week into push, pull, legs and mobility days, and each day walks you set by set with the rest timed. All you have to do is show up.
feature.training.heroAlt: Today's workout screen: phase, weekday, exercise count, estimated duration and a start button.
feature.training.pathTitle: From the first screen to your first workout
feature.training.pathLead: You do not need to know which routine to pick or how to lay out your week.
feature.training.path1Desc: Your level, what you want to focus on (strength, pull-ups, handstand, full body…) and which days of the week you can train.
feature.training.path2Desc: The catalog surfaces the one that fits your level and your goal, with clear warnings if it asks for a lot of days, needs equipment or is worth checking with your doctor first.
feature.training.path3Desc: Every day with its type and its exercises: push, pull, legs, lower back, mobility and rest. And if on a Tuesday you feel like leg day, you train leg day — the calendar is not in charge.
feature.training.path4Desc: Today shows up at the top with its exercises and its estimated duration. One tap on START and the session takes over.
feature.training.pathLimit: Programs are split into phases that ramp up in difficulty, but moving to the next phase is your call, and today it is done from the web.
feature.training.sessTitle: What happens when you hit START
feature.training.sessLead: The screen holds one thing at a time. This is what you will see, in order.
feature.training.sess1Desc: The exercise name fills the screen, with its reps, the muscles it works and a dot for each set you have done. If you have done it before, it reminds you how many reps you managed last time and suggests one more. If the exercise has a note or a tempo, they show up right there.
feature.training.sess1Actions: Log the set · Edit reps, added weight, effort and note · Open the tutorial · Skip to the next exercise
feature.training.sess2Desc: A ring counts down and tells you what is coming next and which set you are on. It chimes at ten seconds and ticks for the last three. If you add or remove time, the app keeps that rest for that exercise and starts there next time.
feature.training.sess2Actions: −15 s · +15 s · +30 s · Skip the rest
feature.training.sess3Desc: Sessions come in three blocks. When the warm-up is done the app says so and lets you move into the main block; at the end it offers the stretches, which you can skip if you are in a hurry.
feature.training.sess4Title: How it went, in one line
feature.training.sess4Desc: Before closing it shows you the summary — title, sets and minutes — and lets you jot down how you felt. A month from now that line is worth more than any chart.
feature.training.sess5Title: And done: see where your time went
feature.training.sess5Desc: When you finish you get the breakdown of how long each exercise took, longest first, any records you broke and a card ready to send to the group chat.
feature.training.sess5Actions: Share the session · Back to your day
feature.training.sessNote: If you leave halfway through, the session waits for you: when you come back you pick up at the exact set you were on, even from the other device.
feature.training.sessOutro: Everything you log during the session — sets, reps, added weight and minutes — ends up in {{link}}, where it turns into your history, your records and your streaks.
feature.training.sess1Alt: Exercise screen during a session, with the reps, the set dots and the reminder of what you did last time.
feature.training.sess2Alt: Rest screen with the countdown ring, the next exercise announced and the buttons to adjust the time.
feature.training.sess5Alt: Final session screen with the breakdown of how long each exercise took.
feature.training.catTitle: What is inside, without rounding up
feature.training.catLead: The whole catalog ships inside the Android app, so you can search it even with no signal.
feature.training.cat1Desc: Exercises in the catalog, each with its description, the muscles it works and the equipment it needs.
feature.training.cat2Desc: Movement categories: push, pull, legs, core, lower back, full body, mobility and skills.
feature.training.cat3Desc: Equipment filters, starting with “no equipment”. You can see only what you can do today, with what you have.
feature.training.cat4Desc: Muscle groups to filter by when you want to work something specific.
feature.training.cat5Desc: Progression chains ordered by hand, from the easiest version to the hardest.
feature.training.cat6Desc: Exercises placed inside those chains, each with its own rule for moving up.
feature.training.cat7Desc: Steps in the pull-up chain, from hanging off the bar to the one-arm pull-up.
feature.training.catLimit: Most of the catalog comes from open exercise databases; what is curated by hand are the progression chains and the execution notes. Each exercise opens a tutorial on YouTube: the videos are not hosted in the app, and only a handful of exercises have an image of their own.
feature.training.catOffline: Browsing the catalog with no signal is a native-app thing; what does and does not get saved when you lose connection is covered in {{link}}.
feature.training.progTitle: How you know it is time to step up
feature.training.progLead: Two mechanisms, and both are concrete numbers instead of feelings.
feature.training.prog1Title: One more rep than last time
feature.training.prog1Desc: As soon as an exercise has history, the first set reminds you what you did last time and suggests one more rep. If you did it with added weight, it suggests 2.5 kg more. It works with any exercise you have ever logged.
feature.training.prog2Title: The next step in the chain
feature.training.prog2Desc: Catalog exercises that belong to a chain have a rep target. When you hit it in three sessions in a row, the “ready to advance” badge shows up along with the next exercise, one notch harder.
feature.training.progTableTitle: The bar rises with the level
feature.training.prog1Reps: 15 reps in 3 sessions in a row
feature.training.prog2Reps: 12 reps in 3 sessions in a row
feature.training.prog3Reps: 10 reps in 3 sessions in a row
feature.training.prog4Reps: 8 reps in 3 sessions in a row
feature.training.progLimit: Chains work with catalog exercises. Inside an official program the prompt you will see is the extra-rep one, which works on all of them.
feature.training.progOutro: The records you break along the way are saved automatically and live in {{link}}.
feature.training.progAlt: Exercise showing the ready-to-advance badge and the steps of its progression chain.
feature.training.ownTitle: When the plan does not fit
feature.training.ownLead: A program is a helping hand, not a sentence. There are three ways out.
feature.training.own1Desc: You pick whichever exercises you want from the catalog and the app works out what kind of day it is from the muscles you chose, so it can suggest a warm-up and stretches already timed. When you finish it is saved as a template you can repeat with one tap.
feature.training.own2Desc: You trained at the park without pulling your phone out: log the workout by hand, with its date, and it still counts towards your history and your streak.
feature.training.own3Desc: The editor walks you through four steps — info, phases, days and exercises — and fills in the warm-up on its own based on the day type. You can also duplicate an official program and tweak it to suit you.
feature.training.ownLimit: Logging a workout with a past date and sharing a program by link are web-only for now. And opening a shared program requires an account.
feature.training.ownCircuits: If what you are after is working in rounds and against the clock instead of by sets, that lives separately: see {{link}}.
feature.training.platLead: Training works on both. What changes is the setup, which is more comfortable on the web, and the company during the session, which is better on the phone.
feature.training.plat1: Pick a program and train the guided session
feature.training.plat2: Resume the session on the other device
feature.training.plat3: See every phase and the exercises of each day
feature.training.plat4: Log sets outside the guided session
feature.training.plat5: Log the set from the notification, with the phone locked
feature.training.plat6: Search the full catalog with no connection
feature.training.plat8: Move the program to another phase
feature.training.plat9: Log a workout with a past date
feature.training.platNote: The Android app is installed from the direct download. There is no published iOS version yet, so that column stays empty even though the code is the same.
feature.training.faq1q: Does it work if I have never trained?
feature.training.faq1a: Yes. Beginner programs start with push-ups — and the note tells you to do them from your knees if full ones are not there yet — and with the Australian row, done on a low bar with your feet on the ground. On top of that, most movements have an easier version to fall back on.
feature.training.faq2q: Do I need a bar or a gym?
feature.training.faq2a: Not to start. You can filter the catalog by the equipment you have, starting with “no equipment”, and see only the exercises you can do today. A bar, parallel bars, rings or added weight open up more, but they are not the starting point.
feature.training.faq3q: Do I have to train on the day the program says?
feature.training.faq3a: No. The week is a guide: you can open any day and train it whenever you want. Today is marked, but nothing forces you to follow it.
feature.training.faq4q: What if I get interrupted halfway through a session?
feature.training.faq4a: The session saves itself with every set. You can leave, do something else and come back to the exact set you were on, even from the other device if you started on the computer and continue on your phone.
feature.training.faq5q: Can I create my own program?
feature.training.faq5a: Yes, with the four-step editor, on the web and on your phone: you define the phases, the days and the exercises of each day. You can also duplicate an official program and change it. Sharing it with someone by link is done from the web, and whoever opens it will need an account.
feature.training.faq6a: The exercise catalog ships inside the Android app, so you can browse it with no data. Logging your sets does need a connection to save to your account: {{link}} explains what holds up and what does not.
feature.nutrition.name: Nutrition and pantry
feature.nutrition.title: From what you have to what you eat.
feature.nutrition.lead: Log meals in seconds, track macros and water, keep your pantry up to date and get recipes made from what is already in your kitchen.
feature.nutrition.card: Meal logging, macros, an AI pantry, saved recipes and a shopping list with cost per meal.
feature.nutrition.whatTitle: From the shop to the plate, without spreadsheets
feature.nutrition.b1d: Add meals by searching the food, scanning a barcode or taking a photo of the plate: AI estimates the contents and you confirm or correct it.
feature.nutrition.b2t: The day's macros, calories and water
feature.nutrition.b2d: Your targets adjust to your goal and your training phase. Calories, protein, carbs, fat and glasses of water all on one screen.
feature.nutrition.b3t: A pantry that understands plain language
feature.nutrition.b3d: Write "bought 2 kg of chicken for $8" and your inventory updates. The pantry knows what you have, what is about to expire and what ran out.
feature.nutrition.b4d: Ask for recipes using what you already have, save your favorites to repeat them and generate the list of what is missing with an estimated cost per meal.
feature.nutrition.howNote: Food does not live apart: your targets move with your training phase and everything you log shows up together in the calendar.
feature.nutrition.s1: Log what you eat — search, barcode or photo.
feature.nutrition.s2: Save what you buy into the pantry.
feature.nutrition.s3: Ask for a recipe and build the shopping list.
feature.nutrition.q1: Do I have to weigh everything?
feature.nutrition.a1: No. You can log by servings or units. The app shows you the trend across the week rather than the exact number for a single day.
feature.nutrition.q2: Does it work with food from my country?
feature.nutrition.a2: Yes. Search by name, scan the product barcode or describe the dish in your own words and adjust the result if needed.
feature.nutrition.q3: Does the AI decide my diet?
feature.nutrition.a3: No. It suggests recipes and estimates values; you confirm every entry. These are estimates and patterns, not medical advice or a clinical plan.
feature.progress.name: Progress and insights
feature.progress.title: Progress becomes obvious.
feature.progress.lead: A calendar with everything you did, charts per exercise, before and after photos, personal records and a weekly summary that connects your habits.
feature.progress.card: Unified calendar, per-exercise charts, progress photos, records and a weekly summary.
feature.progress.b1d: Workouts, cardio, meals, sleep, water and weight in the same monthly view. Tap a day and see exactly what happened.
feature.progress.b2t: Charts by exercise and by body
feature.progress.b2d: Sets and volume per exercise, body weight, measurements and a 1RM calculator. That is how you tell progress apart from repetition.
feature.progress.b3d: When you beat your mark the app celebrates it and stores it. Progress photos sit side by side so you see what the scale does not show.
feature.progress.b4t: A weekly summary across your data
feature.progress.b4d: A summary that connects sleep, training and nutrition: what went well, what to watch and one concrete suggestion for next week.
feature.progress.howNote: Nothing extra to log: progress fills itself from the sessions, meals and cardio you already do.
feature.progress.s1: Train and log your sets as usual.
feature.progress.s2: Add weight, measurements or a photo whenever you want.
feature.progress.s3: Check your week and your month at a glance.
feature.progress.q1: How long until I see something?
feature.progress.a1: Charts need a couple of sessions with logged sets. The weekly summary needs a few days of data before it starts finding patterns.
feature.progress.q2: Who can see my progress photos?
feature.progress.a2: Only you. Photos, measurements and health data are private to your account; what friends see is your training activity.
feature.progress.q3: Is the weekly summary medical advice?
feature.progress.a3: No. These are patterns observed in your own logs, with no causes or diagnoses — a hint for your next adjustment, nothing more.
feature.cardio.name: GPS cardio
feature.cardio.card: Running, walking and cycling with live GPS, a route map and a shareable session card.
feature.cardio.metaTitle: GPS cardio: route, pace and splits
feature.cardio.metaDesc: Track running, walking or cycling with GPS: route on the map, pace, splits and elevation. On Android it keeps recording with the screen locked.
feature.cardio.h1: Your route on the map, kilometre by kilometre.
feature.cardio.heroLead: Running, walking and cycling with GPS: distance, pace, splits and elevation while you move. On Android the session keeps recording with the screen locked, and you can pause it from the notification without unlocking the phone.
feature.cardio.heroBadge: Android · keeps recording in the background
feature.cardio.shot1Alt: Detail of a running session: the route drawn on the map with distance, duration and average pace.
feature.cardio.measureTitle: What it measures, and where each number comes from
feature.cardio.measureLead: None of this is a marketing estimate: every number follows a rule, and here they all are.
feature.cardio.m1Source: Distance between GPS points smoothed with a Kalman filter.
feature.cardio.m1Note: Fixes with accuracy worse than 20 m are dropped, and so is any movement under 3 m: standing still, the kilometres do not go up.
feature.cardio.m2Source: The speed field reported by the GPS, only above 0.5 m/s.
feature.cardio.m2Note: It is the device instant speed, not distance over time: that is why it reacts fast on hills.
feature.cardio.m3Source: One per full kilometre, plus a partial one if more than 100 m are left at the end.
feature.cardio.m3Note: The partial split is normalised to min/km so you can compare it with the rest.
feature.cardio.m4Source: The sum of every altitude increase the GPS reports.
feature.cardio.m4Note: No barometer and no smoothing: treat it as a rough figure, not a precise one.
feature.cardio.m5Source: The fastest 200 m stretch of the whole session.
feature.cardio.m5Note: It is not "your best kilometre": it is a 200 m sliding window.
feature.cardio.m6Source: A three-point moving average over the GPS speed.
feature.cardio.m6Note: That way a single bad fix does not gift you a sprint you never ran.
feature.cardio.m7Source: The activity MET × your weight × duration.
feature.cardio.m7Note: It is an estimate: in the same time, 3 km and 5 km give the same figure. With no weight on record it assumes 70 kg.
feature.cardio.m8Source: From your watch, via Health Connect, once the session is already saved.
feature.cardio.m8Note: Android only, and only if the time window matches. Never live.
feature.cardio.runTitle: You start it, pocket the phone and the session carries on
feature.cardio.runLead: This is a full session in the Android app, from the start button to the shareable card.
feature.cardio.run1Desc: One button and you are recording. If today is a cardio day in your program, the screen says so and it gets marked as done when you finish.
feature.cardio.run2Desc: The split in progress, GPS accuracy with a traffic light and the map drawing itself underneath as you go.
feature.cardio.run3Desc: Kilometres and pace kept up to date, a stopwatch that runs on its own and a button to pause without unlocking the phone. If the system kills the app, the session picks up where it was when you reopen it.
feature.cardio.run4Title: Map, splits and a card to send
feature.cardio.run4Desc: Full route, elevation profile, calories, elevation gain and best pace, the splits table and room for your note. The card with your route takes one tap.
feature.cardio.runKmHaptic: Every completed kilometre gives you a vibration: with the phone in your pocket it is the only cue that gets through.
feature.cardio.runOutro: Cardio counts like any other workout: it shows up in your activity, in your calendar and in {{link}}.
feature.cardio.actTitle: Running, walking and riding are not measured the same
feature.cardio.actLead: The app changes the units, the route colour and the plausibility thresholds depending on what you are doing.
feature.cardio.actNote: On a bike the whole session switches from min/km to km/h. And snapping the route to the streets, which only exists on the web, uses the driving profile: the public routing service has no cycling profile.
feature.cardio.gapTitle: When the GPS fails, we tell you
feature.cardio.gapLead: A tunnel, a building, your pocket. Losing signal happens: what changes is what the app does next.
feature.cardio.gapBeforeDesc: Join the two ends of the gap with a straight line and hand you those kilometres as if you had run them.
feature.cardio.gapAfterDesc: It marks the stretch as a gap after 30 seconds without signal, draws it dashed on the map and only adds that distance if the implied speed is plausible for your activity. If the track is not clean, the kilometres show a tilde and a warning with how many gaps there were.
feature.cardio.qualityGoodDesc: Not a single gap and at least 10 points per kilometre. The numbers stand as they are.
feature.cardio.qualityEstimatedDesc: There was a gap, or fewer than 10 points per kilometre. Distance is shown as approximate.
feature.cardio.qualityPoorDesc: More than 20% of the distance comes from gaps, or fewer than 3 points per kilometre. Warning in red.
feature.cardio.gapLimit: If no fix has come in after 15 seconds, the app restarts the GPS on its own. And if it is the connection that fails, the session is kept on the phone and uploaded when it can — with two limits worth knowing: the queue holds 5 unsent sessions and an active session expires after 24 hours. More on {{link}}.
feature.cardio.platTitle: What changes depending on where you use it
feature.cardio.platLead: The web records with GPS as long as you keep it open, and on top of that it snaps the route to the streets and exports GPX. The Android app is the one that survives a locked screen.
feature.cardio.p2: Keeps recording with the screen locked
feature.cardio.p3: Notification with metrics and a stopwatch
feature.cardio.p4: Pause and resume from the notification
feature.cardio.p6: Map, elevation profile and splits table
feature.cardio.p8: Export GPX of the session you just finished
feature.cardio.p9: Heart rate and calories from your watch
feature.cardio.p10: Home screen widget with the week kilometres
feature.cardio.p12: Saved if the connection fails, recovered if the app closes
feature.cardio.platNote: There is no iPhone app yet, and the Android one installs as an APK: it is not on Google Play.
feature.cardio.limitTitle: What it still does not do
feature.cardio.limit1: There is no iPhone app. On iOS you cannot record in the background and there is no build to install.
feature.cardio.limit2: On the web the GPS only records with the tab open and visible: it is not a replacement for the app when you head outside.
feature.cardio.limit3: There is no auto-pause, no pace alerts, no manual laps and no cardio intervals.
feature.cardio.limit4: There is no live heart rate, no Bluetooth sensors and no cadence.
feature.cardio.limit5: You cannot plan routes or follow a route loaded beforehand.
feature.cardio.limit6: GPX is exported from the web only, and only for the session you just finished. There is no import, no Strava and no Garmin.
feature.cardio.limit7: A session link asks for an account to open: to send it to someone outside, use the card.
feature.cardio.fq1: Does it really keep recording with the phone in my pocket?
feature.cardio.fa1: On Android it does: the session runs in a foreground service with a persistent notification, so the system does not cut it off and you can pause it from the lock screen. On the web it does not: if you lock the phone or switch apps, the browser suspends the page.
feature.cardio.fa2: Quite a bit more than a strength session: the GPS asks for a position every second in navigation mode and the screen stays on during the session. We do not quote percentages because we have not measured them properly.
feature.cardio.fq3: What happens if I lose signal or the app closes?
feature.cardio.fa3: Losing signal opens a gap: it is drawn dashed and that distance only counts if it is plausible. If the app closes, the session is restored from a save made every 5 seconds. And with no connection it stays on the phone and uploads later — the queue holds 5 sessions and an active session expires after 24 hours.
feature.cardio.fq4: Do races against friends use this same GPS?
feature.cardio.fa4: No. {{link}} have their own tracking, more forgiving and simpler: it only adds distance inside the competition time window, with no splits and no elevation.
feature.cardio.fq5: Can I take my data with me?
feature.cardio.fa5: From the web you can download the GPX of the session you just finished. Exporting the full history or syncing with Strava or Garmin is not there yet.

feature.circuits.b3d: Work, rest between exercises, rest between rounds and number of rounds. The setup is saved so you can repeat it.

feature.circuits.s3: Hit start and follow the timer.
feature.circuits.q1: Does it work for HIIT or Tabata?
feature.circuits.a1: Yes. Timed mode is exactly that: blocks of work and rest repeated for as many rounds as you define.
feature.circuits.a2: Yes. Mark it done early or skip it, and the circuit moves to the next one without breaking the timer.
feature.circuits.q3: Does it count towards my streak?

feature.races.name: Races
feature.races.card: Races with a lobby, a live distance board and shareable results.
feature.races.metaDesc: Create a race, share the link and everyone runs wherever they are: synced start, live GPS board and final results when the window closes.
feature.races.h1: Run together. From wherever you are.
feature.races.heroLead: A race is a shared time window: the creator starts it, everyone sets off on the same second and each phone’s GPS counts the kilometres. Nobody has to show up at the same park.
feature.races.heroAlt: Live race board with three runners and the remaining time
feature.races.lifeTitle: Four states, from the invite to the podium
feature.races.lifeLead: A race goes through four screens. Here is what every participant sees on each one, and what they can do.
feature.races.life1Desc: The race name and its target up top; below, the participant list growing live and who has already tapped Ready. Creating the race does not sign you up: the creator taps Join too. One participant is enough to start, because Ready blocks nothing.
feature.races.life1Actions: Join · Tap Ready (guests) · Share the link or show the QR · Start and Cancel, creator only
feature.races.life1Alt: Race lobby with three participants and the join button
feature.races.life2Desc: The creator starts the race and a full-screen countdown takes over, with a tick and a vibration. There is a single start time for the whole race, stored on the server: it is not a stopwatch per person.
feature.races.life2Actions: You can still join during the countdown; once it is running, you cannot
feature.races.life2Alt: Full-screen start countdown showing the number three in lime green
feature.races.life3Title: Your phone counts, the board reorders
feature.races.life3Desc: Kilometres, time —or what is left, if the race is on the clock— and pace up top; the progress bar towards the target; below, the standings and the map showing who is where. Your progress reaches everyone else every three seconds, and on the web a sound tells you when your position changes.
feature.races.life3Actions: Leave · Finish the race: on the web only the creator, on Android everyone sees the button
feature.races.life3Alt: Live race with your own stats, progress bar and standings
feature.races.life4Title: Podium, then straight to the group chat
feature.races.life4Desc: Who won, the race time and the full standings with the DNFs at the bottom. Anyone who leaves or falls short shows up as DNF, not with a half-finished distance. From here you can {{link}} so the race counts in your history.
feature.races.life4Actions: Save as workout · Export GPX and results card, web only
feature.races.life4Alt: Race results with the winner, the standings and one DNF participant
feature.races.lifeNote: There is a fifth state that is not shown above because nobody sees it: if the creator cancels before the start, the race closes and no result is recorded.
feature.races.linkTitle: One link and they are in
feature.races.linkLead: No codes and no private rooms to set up: a race is a web address you share.
feature.races.link1Desc: From the lobby anyone can copy the link, open the system share sheet or, on the web, show a QR code to be scanned with a phone camera.
feature.races.link2Desc: If you marked the race public, pasting the link into WhatsApp or Telegram shows a preview with the real name and target, generated by the server. If it is private, nothing leaks.
feature.races.link3Title: You need an account to see it
feature.races.link3Desc: The link is public, but whoever opens it without signing in only gets a login screen: no name, no target, no participants. Creating the account is free and takes a minute.
feature.races.linkLimit: You can get in until the last second of the countdown. Once the race is under way you cannot: a latecomer could not be ranked fairly.
feature.races.boardLead: The standings reorder while you run. These are the columns, and the rule that decides the winner.
feature.races.board1Desc: Current position. Those who finished first, then those still running, and the DNFs at the bottom.
feature.races.board2Desc: The name they joined with, with the leader mark and your own row highlighted in lime.
feature.races.board3Desc: Minutes per kilometre, computed from the distance and time each phone reports.
feature.races.board4Desc: Time in the race, measured against the server clock rather than the phone’s.
feature.races.board5Desc: Distance covered to two decimals, plus the coloured dot telling you whether they are still running or already done.
feature.races.rankTitle: Who wins, depending on the race type
feature.races.rank1Rule: Whoever completes the distance first: finish time decides.
feature.races.rank2Mode: On the clock, or with no target distance
feature.races.rank2Rule: Whoever covers the most distance. Ties break on pace, and then alphabetically, so the board does not jitter.
feature.races.rank3Rule: Anyone who leaves or falls short shows as DNF, always at the bottom of the board.
feature.races.robustTitle: Built for a park, not a laboratory
feature.races.robustLead: Patchy coverage, a phone with the wrong clock, a tab that reloads. Here is what the app does about it.
feature.races.robust1Desc: The start, your time and every point of your route are computed against the server clock, measured when you enter the race. Two phones with skewed clocks compete on equal terms.
feature.races.robust2Desc: GPS does not need data: your route keeps recording on the phone, and failed uploads retry after one second, three and nine. When the connection returns, your position catches up.
feature.races.robust3Desc: Every upload saves a local copy of your distance and your trace. Reload the page mid-race and it picks up from there instead of reporting zero kilometres.
feature.races.robust4Desc: Readings with more than 30 metres of error are ignored entirely, and jumps of more than 500 metres between two readings never count towards your distance.
feature.races.robustLimit: Three limits worth knowing before you bet anything on it. A race needs the app in the foreground with the screen on: there is no background tracking, that is what {{link}} is for. If someone loses coverage, everyone else sees them frozen at their last distance, with no warning. And closing the race is triggered by a phone with the screen open, not by the server: if everybody closes the app halfway, the race stays open.
feature.races.vsTitle: They are not the same thing
feature.races.vsLead: A race is a time window with GPS. A challenge is a goal you accumulate against a deadline. If the problem is that you never manage to be free at the same hour, what you want is a challenge.
feature.races.vs1Challenge: An accumulated metric: sessions, pull-ups, push-ups, streak or one you define
feature.races.vs2Race: A window of up to three hours
feature.races.vs2Challenge: A week, two, a month or the dates you set
feature.races.vs3Race: Synced: a seven-second countdown for everyone
feature.races.vs3Challenge: It begins on the start date, no ceremony
feature.races.vs4Aspect: Do you have to be there
feature.races.vs4Race: Yes: you run live, with the app open
feature.races.vs4Challenge: No: it adds up from whatever you train, whenever you can
feature.races.vs5Race: No. Races do not send any notification yet
feature.races.vs5Challenge: Yes: you get a notification when someone joins your challenge
feature.races.vsOutro: Would you rather have a goal that adds up on its own over a month? {{link}}.
feature.races.platTitle: What you can do on each platform
feature.races.platLead: Creating, joining, running and competing work the same on the web and on Android. What differs is the extras around them.
feature.races.plat1: Create a race and join by link
feature.races.plat3: Start countdown with sound and vibration
feature.races.plat5: Draw the route when creating the race
feature.races.plat7: Sound alert when your position changes
feature.races.plat9: Shareable results card and GPX export
feature.races.platNote: The Android app installs from a direct download. We mark nothing for iOS: the code is the same, but until there is a published download we are not going to present it as available.
feature.races.faq1q: Do we have to run in the same place?
feature.races.faq1a: No. Everyone runs wherever they are; what you share is the time window. What gets compared is whatever each phone’s GPS measures inside that window.
feature.races.faq2a: It depends on the type. If you set a target distance, whoever completes it first wins. If the race is on the clock, or you set no distance, whoever covers the most kilometres wins, and pace breaks the tie.
feature.races.faq3q: What if I lose signal halfway?
feature.races.faq3a: GPS does not need data, so your route keeps recording and failed uploads retry on their own. Your position on the board catches up as soon as the connection is back. In the meantime everyone else sees you frozen at your last distance.
feature.races.faq4q: Can I join a race that already started?
feature.races.faq4a: You can get in until the last second of the countdown. Once it is running, no: a latecomer could not be ranked fairly.
feature.races.faq5q: Can someone without an account watch the race?
feature.races.faq5a: No. The link is public and generates a preview if the race is public, but to see the race —and to compete— you need to sign in. It is free.
feature.races.faq6q: Can I lock my phone while I run?
feature.races.faq6a: Not in a race yet: tracking needs the app in the foreground, though the screen stays on by itself. To run with the phone in your pocket, use {{link}}.
feature.challenges.name: Challenges
feature.challenges.title: Challenges that make you show up.
feature.challenges.lead: A goal, a deadline and your friends pushing on the same board — with progress that fills itself in.
feature.challenges.card: Challenges with a goal and deadline, shared progress and a nudge when someone moves.
feature.challenges.b1t: Set the goal and the deadline
feature.challenges.b1d: A number — reps, sessions, distance — and a closing date. There is nothing else to configure.
feature.challenges.b2d: Share the challenge with your friends or with a link; everyone sees their own progress and everyone else’s on the same screen.
feature.challenges.b3d: What you train counts towards the challenge without logging anything extra: the bar climbs as the days go by.
feature.challenges.b4d: Ongoing challenges stay separate from the ones that ended, so you keep the record of what you pulled off together.
feature.challenges.howNote: For now challenges are created from the web version; on Android you can join, progress and follow them as normal.
feature.challenges.s1: Create the challenge with its goal and date.
feature.challenges.s3: Train — the progress adds up on its own.
feature.challenges.a1: Yes. A challenge with no invitees works as a personal goal with a deadline and a progress bar.
feature.challenges.a2: They are created from the web version. On Android you can join, follow the progress and compete with no limitations.
feature.challenges.a3: The challenge moves to "finished" with each participant’s result, and you can start the next one in a tap.
feature.community.name: Community
feature.community.title: Friends who notice when you show up.
feature.community.lead: Follow your friends, react to their workouts and compete on the weekly board — with blocking and reports so the space stays yours.
feature.community.card: Friends, activity feed, reactions, a weekly leaderboard and blocking and reporting tools.
feature.community.b1d: Find friends by name or username, invite them over WhatsApp with your link and follow their activity from the feed.
feature.community.b2t: A feed with reactions and comments
feature.community.b2d: See who completed which day, with which program and in which phase, and react or comment to push them along.
feature.community.b3d: Sessions, sets and streak among the people you follow. A small board where finishing on top actually means something.
feature.community.b4d: Block someone so they disappear from your feed and you from theirs, and report content so it gets reviewed.
feature.community.howNote: Social is optional: if you would rather train alone, the app works exactly the same following nobody.
feature.community.s2: Follow their activity in the feed.
feature.community.q1: What exactly can my friends see?
feature.community.a1: Your training activity: completed sessions, streaks, records and challenges. Not your progress photos, measurements or health data.
feature.community.q2: Can I use the app with no social at all?
feature.community.a2: Yes. Friends, feed and leaderboard are optional; if you follow nobody, those screens simply stay empty.
feature.community.a3: You can block them — they stop seeing your activity and vanish from yours — and report the content so we review it.
feature.offline.name: Offline and in sync
feature.offline.title: No signal in the basement. No excuses.
feature.offline.lead: The app works without internet and syncs itself when you are back. Start on the web, finish on Android: your progress travels with you.
feature.offline.card: Works offline, syncs when you are back and keeps your active session across Android and the web.
feature.offline.whatTitle: The app does not depend on your coverage
feature.offline.b1d: Your sessions, sets and logs are stored on the phone even with no signal in the gym basement or out in the park.
feature.offline.b2d: Once you are back online everything you did uploads without you pressing anything or remembering what was pending.
feature.offline.b3t: The same session on two screens
feature.offline.b3d: Start a workout on the web and pick it up on Android right where you left off: the active session syncs between devices.
feature.offline.b4t: Install it like any other app
feature.offline.b4d: On Android there is a native app, and in the browser you can install it to your home screen as a PWA — same account either way.
feature.offline.howNote: It is the same account on both sides: nothing to export, import or migrate between devices.
feature.offline.s1: Install the app on Android or in the browser.
feature.offline.s3: When you are back online, it all uploads itself.
feature.offline.q1: Do I lose the workout if the app closes?
feature.offline.a1: No. What you have done is saved locally right away and the active session is restored when you open it again.
feature.offline.a2: No. The Android app installs from the official APK published in our repository, and the web version runs in any modern browser.
feature.offline.a3: There is no native iOS app yet, but you can use the web version from Safari and install it to your home screen.
